Relative Density Ratio Optimization for
Stable and Statistically Consistent Model Alignment

Hiroshi Takahashi ††thanks: Corresponding author: hiroshibm.takahashi@ntt.com Affiliation: NTT, Inc.    Tomoharu Iwata Affiliation: NTT, Inc.    Atsutoshi Kumagai Affiliation: NTT, Inc.    Sekitoshi Kanai Affiliation: NTT, Inc.    Masanori Yamada Affiliation: NTT DOCOMO, INC.    Kosuke Nishida Affiliation: NTT, Inc.    Kazutoshi Shinoda Affiliation: NTT, Inc.
Abstract

Aligning language models with human preferences is essential for ensuring their safety and reliability. Although most existing approaches assume specific human preference models such as the Bradley-Terry model, this assumption may fail to accurately capture true human preferences, and consequently, these methods lack statistical consistency, i.e., the guarantee that language models converge to the true human preference as the number of samples increases. In contrast, direct density ratio optimization (DDRO) achieves statistical consistency without assuming any human preference models. DDRO models the density ratio between preferred and non-preferred data distributions using the language model, and then optimizes it via density ratio estimation. However, this density ratio is unstable and often diverges, leading to training instability of DDRO. In this paper, we propose a novel alignment method that is both stable and statistically consistent. Our approach is based on the relative density ratio between the preferred data distribution and a mixture of the preferred and non-preferred data distributions. Our approach is stable since this relative density ratio is bounded above and does not diverge. Moreover, it is statistically consistent and yields significantly tighter convergence guarantees than DDRO. We experimentally show its effectiveness with Qwen 2.5 and Llama 3.

1 Introduction

Language models have demonstrated remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, such as text generation, translation, question answering, and information retrieval (Vaswani et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2020; Achiam et al., 2023). Nevertheless, they can also generate outputs that are undesirable for humans, such as inaccurate information (Ji et al., 2023), harmful content (Bender et al., 2021), and biased statements (Sheng et al., 2019; Gehman et al., 2020). This may threaten the safety and reliability of language models.

Alignment, which tunes language models to follow human preferences using a preference dataset containing preferred and non-preferred responses to various prompts, is essential for ensuring safety and reliability (Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023; Ethayarajh et al., 2024). To model human preferences, most existing approaches assume the Bradley-Terry model (Bradley and Terry, 1952), which is widely used in learning to rank. For example, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) (Ouyang et al., 2022) first trains a reward model using the preference dataset under the Bradley-Terry assumption, and then tunes the language model via reinforcement learning to maximize the reward-model score. Direct preference optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) shows that the reward model can be represented by the language model, and aligns the language model through training the reward model without reinforcement learning. In contrast, Kahneman-Tversky optimization (KTO) (Ethayarajh et al., 2024) uses prospect theory (Tversky and Kahneman, 1992; Kahneman and Tversky, 2013) to model human preferences, which captures how humans make decisions under uncertainty. KTO can be regarded as a generalization of DPO.

Although these approaches are powerful, since human preference models may not capture the real complexities of human preference accurately (Wu et al., 2022), they lack statistical consistency (Vapnik, 1999; Mohri et al., 2018), i.e., the guarantee that the language model converges to the true human preference as the number of samples increases (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025). To address this, direct density ratio optimization (DDRO) (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025) presents an alignment approach without assuming any human preference models. DDRO is based on density ratio estimation, which directly estimates the ratio between two distributions. DDRO models the density ratio between the preferred and non-preferred data distributions using the language model, and optimizes the language model through density ratio estimation. In contrast to other alignment approaches, DDRO satisfies statistical consistency. However, it has been empirically observed that training tends to be unstable (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025).

Our purpose is to propose an alignment method that is both stable and statistically consistent by addressing the instability of DDRO. One reason for the instability of DDRO lies in the instability of the density ratio. Although DDRO models the density ratio between the preferred and non-preferred data distributions, it may diverge when the supports of these two distributions, the regions where their values are non-zero, are different (Sugiyama et al., 2012). Since preferred and non-preferred responses are likely to have different supports, this density ratio may diverge, leading to instability in DDRO. To address this, we employ a more stable approach called relative density ratio estimation (Yamada et al., 2013). The relative density ratio is defined as the ratio between the preferred data distribution and a mixture of the preferred and non-preferred data distributions. Unlike the ordinary density ratio, the relative density ratio is bounded above and does not diverge, enabling more stable estimation. We model the relative density ratio using the language model, and optimize the language model through relative density ratio estimation. We theoretically show that the proposed method is more stable, statistically consistent, and yields significantly tighter convergence guarantees than DDRO.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose a novel alignment method called relative density ratio optimization (RDRO), which is based on relative density ratio estimation (Yamada et al., 2013).

  • •

    We theoretically show that our RDRO is more stable, statistically consistent, and yields significantly tighter convergence guarantees than DDRO.

  • •

    We demonstrate the effectiveness of our RDRO with Qwen 2.5 (Team et al., 2024) and Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024).

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Problem Setup

Let xx be the prompt and yy be the response. Given a preferred dataset 𝒟+=(xn+,yn+)n=1N\mathcal{D}^{+}=\left(x_{n}^{+},y_{n}^{+}\right)_{n=1}^{N} and a non-preferred dataset 𝒟−=(xm−,ym−)m=1M\mathcal{D}^{-}=\left(x_{m}^{-},y_{m}^{-}\right)_{m=1}^{M}, we assume that 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+} follows preferred data distribution p+​(x,y)=p+​(y|x)​p​(x)p^{+}(x,y)=p^{+}(y|x)p(x), and 𝒟−\mathcal{D}^{-} follows non-preferred data distribution p−​(x,y)=p−​(y|x)​p​(x)p^{-}(x,y)=p^{-}(y|x)p(x). Note that we assume the same prompt distribution: p⁡(x)p(x) for both datasets, while the response distributions given prompts: p+​(y|x)p^{+}(y|x) and p−​(y|x)p^{-}(y|x) differ. Let pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) be the policy of the language model to be aligned (e.g., a pre-trained or supervised fine-tuning model) with parameter θ\theta, and pref​(y|x)p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x) be the reference policy, which serves as a regularizer for pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) and is typically set to a frozen copy of the initial pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x). Our goal is to align pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) with p+​(y|x)p^{+}(y|x) using 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+}, 𝒟−\mathcal{D}^{-}, and pref​(y|x)p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x).

2.2 Direct Density Ratio Optimization

Direct density ratio optimization (DDRO) (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025) tries to align the policy pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) with the true preference p+​(y|x)p^{+}(y|x) using density ratio estimation (Sugiyama et al., 2012). DDRO assumes that the reference policy pref​(y|x)p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x) can be written as follows:

pref​(y|x)=α​p+​(y|x)+(1−α)​p−​(y|x),\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)=\alpha p^{+}(y|x)+(1-\alpha)p^{-}(y|x), (1)

where α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) is a hyperparameter. This assumption can be interpreted as labeling the response of the reference policy pref​(y|x)p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x) as preferred with probability α\alpha and as non-preferred with probability 1−α1-\alpha. With this assumption, the following relation holds between the reference policy pref​(y|x)p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x) and the true preference p+​(y|x)p^{+}(y|x):

pref​(y|x)p+​(y|x)=α​p+​(y|x)+(1−α)​p−​(y|x)p+​(y|x)=α+(1−α)​p−​(y|x)p+​(y|x).\displaystyle\frac{p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)}{p^{+}(y|x)}=\frac{\alpha p^{+}(y|x)+(1-\alpha)p^{-}(y|x)}{p^{+}(y|x)}=\alpha+(1-\alpha)\frac{p^{-}(y|x)}{p^{+}(y|x)}. (2)

Accordingly, the density ratio p−​(y|x)/p+​(y|x)p^{-}(y|x)/p^{+}(y|x) is written as follows:

p−​(y|x)p+​(y|x)=11−α​pref​(y|x)p+​(y|x)−α1−α≡g∗​(y|x).\displaystyle\frac{p^{-}(y|x)}{p^{+}(y|x)}=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\frac{p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)}{p^{+}(y|x)}-\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\equiv g^{*}(y|x). (3)

By replacing the true preference p+​(y|x)p^{+}(y|x) with the policy pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x), this density ratio is modeled as follows:

gθ​(y|x)≡11−α​pref​(y|x)pθ​(y|x)−α1−α.\displaystyle g_{\theta}(y|x)\equiv\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\frac{p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)}{p_{\theta}(y|x)}-\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}. (4)

DDRO tries to align pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) with p+​(y|x)p^{+}(y|x) by minimizing the Bregman divergence (Sugiyama et al., 2012) between g∗​(y|x)g^{*}(y|x) and gθ​(y|x)g_{\theta}(y|x):

ℒDRE(θ)=𝔼p+​(x,y)[Bregf(g∗(y|x)∥gθ(y|x))],\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DRE}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}(x,y)}\left[\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(g^{*}(y|x)\|g_{\theta}(y|x)\right)\right], (5)

where

Bregf(u∥v)=f(u)−f(v)−f′(v)(u−v),\displaystyle\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(u\|v\right)=f(u)-f(v)-f^{\prime}(v)(u-v), (6)

𝔼⁡[⋅]\mathbb{E}[\cdot] is the expectation, f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is a differentiable and strictly convex function, and f′f^{\prime} is the derivative of ff.

When f⁡(t)=t​log⁡t−(1+t)​log⁡(1+t)f(t)=t\log t-(1+t)\log(1+t), this optimization problem can be reduced to the logistic regression problem (Sugiyama et al., 2012):

ℒDRE​(θ)=𝔼p+​(x,y)​[log⁡(1+gθ​(y|x))]+𝔼p−​(x,y)​[log⁡(1+1/gθ​(y|x))].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DRE}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}(x,y)}\left[\log(1+g_{\theta}(y|x))\right]+\mathbb{E}_{p^{-}(x,y)}\left[\log(1+1/g_{\theta}(y|x))\right]. (7)

Using the datasets 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+} and 𝒟−\mathcal{D}^{-}, ℒDRE​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DRE}}(\theta) is approximated as follows:

1N​∑n=1Nlog⁡(1+gθ​(yn+|xn+))+1M​∑m=1Mlog⁡(1+1/gθ​(ym−|xm−)).\displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\log(1+g_{\theta}(y_{n}^{+}|x_{n}^{+}))+\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\log(1+1/g_{\theta}(y_{m}^{-}|x_{m}^{-})). (8)

Unfortunately, this optimization is unstable in practice due to gradient spikes (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025). To mitigate this, DDRO heuristically applies a monotonically increasing function S⁡(t)=log⁡σ⁡(t)S(t)=\log\sigma(t), where σ⁡(t)=1/(1+exp⁡(−t))\sigma(t)=1/(1+\exp(-t)) is the sigmoid function, to this objective as follows:

ℒ^DRE​(θ)=1N​∑n=1NS⁡(log⁡(1+gθ​(yn+|xn+)))+1M​∑m=1MS⁡(log⁡(1+1/gθ​(ym−|xm−))).\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{DRE}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}S(\log(1+g_{\theta}(y_{n}^{+}|x_{n}^{+})))+\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}S(\log(1+1/g_{\theta}(y_{m}^{-}|x_{m}^{-}))). (9)

Since just minimizing this objective will lead to catastrophic forgetting (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), DDRO introduces the regularizer based on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) and pref​(y|x)p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x) as follows:

ℒDDRO(θ)=ℒ^DRE(θ)+βKL(pθ∥pref),\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DDRO}}(\theta)=\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{DRE}}(\theta)+\beta\mathrm{KL}\left(p_{\theta}\|p_{\mathrm{ref}}\right), (10)

where β\beta is a hyperparameter that controls the strength of the regularizer.

DDRO has the following property for the optimal parameter θ∗=arg​minθ⁡ℒDRE​(θ)\theta^{*}=\argmin_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DRE}}(\theta):

ℒDRE​(θ∗)=0⇔gθ∗=g∗⇔pθ∗=p+.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DRE}}(\theta^{*})=0\Leftrightarrow g_{\theta^{*}}=g^{*}\Leftrightarrow p_{\theta^{*}}=p^{+}. (11)

Furthermore, as the number of samples increases, the policy pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) converges to the true preference p+​(y|x)p^{+}(y|x) at the rate of 𝒪⁡(1/N+1/M)\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N}+1/\sqrt{M}). Although DDRO has this ideal statistical consistency, it has been experimentally observed that training still tends to become unstable.

3 Proposed Method

One reason for the instability of DDRO lies in the instability of the density ratio gθ​(y|x)g_{\theta}(y|x). Although gθ​(y|x)g_{\theta}(y|x) models the true density ratio p−​(y|x)/p+​(y|x)p^{-}(y|x)/p^{+}(y|x), it may diverge when the supports of these two distributions, the regions where their values are non-zero, are different. Since the preferred response y+y^{+} and the non-preferred response y−y^{-} are likely to have different supports, the density ratio may diverge, leading to instability in DDRO.

In this section, we propose an alignment method that is both stable and statistically consistent by addressing the instability of DDRO. To this end, we employ a more stable approach called relative density ratio estimation (Yamada et al., 2013), which generalizes density ratio estimation.

3.1 Relative Density Ratio Optimization

First, we define the relative density ratio r∗​(y|x)r^{*}(y|x) as follows:

r∗​(y|x)≡p+​(y|x)pref​(y|x)=p+​(y|x)α​p+​(y|x)+(1−α)​p−​(y|x).\displaystyle r^{*}(y|x)\equiv\frac{p^{+}(y|x)}{p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)}=\frac{p^{+}(y|x)}{\alpha p^{+}(y|x)+(1-\alpha)p^{-}(y|x)}. (12)

This relative density ratio can be regarded as a generalization of the density ratio since it reduces to the standard density ratio when α=0\alpha=0. Figure 1(a) compares the density ratio g∗​(y|x)g^{*}(y|x) and the relative density ratio r∗​(y|x)r^{*}(y|x). By definition, r∗​(y|x)∈[0,1/α]r^{*}(y|x)\in\left[0,1/\alpha\right]. Hence, unlike the density ratio, the relative density ratio does not diverge and can be estimated in a stable manner.

By replacing the true preference p+​(y|x)p^{+}(y|x) with the policy pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x), we model this relative density ratio as follows:

rθ​(y|x)≡pθ​(y|x)pref​(y|x).\displaystyle r_{\theta}(y|x)\equiv\frac{p_{\theta}(y|x)}{p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)}. (13)

Analogous to DDRO, we try to align the policy pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) with the true preference p+​(y|x)p^{+}(y|x) by minimizing the Bregman divergence between r∗​(y|x)r^{*}(y|x) and rθ​(y|x)r_{\theta}(y|x):

ℒRDRE(θ)=𝔼pref​(x,y)[Bregf(r∗(y|x)∥rθ(y|x))],\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x,y)}\left[\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(r^{*}(y|x)\|r_{\theta}(y|x)\right)\right], (14)

where pref​(x,y)=pref​(y|x)​p​(x)p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x,y)=p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)p(x). When f⁡(t)=t​log⁡t−(1+t)​log⁡(1+t)f(t)=t\log t-(1+t)\log(1+t), this optimization problem can be reduced to the logistic regression problem (Sugiyama et al., 2012):

ℒRDRE​(θ)=𝔼pref​(x,y)​[log⁡(1+rθ​(y|x))]+𝔼p+​(x,y)​[log⁡(1+1/rθ​(y|x))].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x,y)}\left[\log(1+r_{\theta}(y|x))\right]+\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}(x,y)}\left[\log(1+1/r_{\theta}(y|x))\right]. (15)

Defining Tθ​(x,y)=log⁡pθ​(y|x)−log⁡pref​(y|x)T_{\theta}(x,y)=\log p_{\theta}(y|x)-\log p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x), we have:

rθ​(y|x)=exp⁡(Tθ​(x,y)).\displaystyle r_{\theta}(y|x)=\exp(T_{\theta}(x,y)). (16)

Substituting this into ℒRDRE​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta), we obtain:

ℒRDRE​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta) =𝔼pref​(x,y)​[log⁡(1+exp⁡(Tθ​(x,y)))]+𝔼p+​(x,y)​[log⁡(1+1/exp⁡(Tθ​(x,y)))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x,y)}\left[\log(1+\exp(T_{\theta}(x,y)))\right]+\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}(x,y)}\left[\log(1+1/\exp(T_{\theta}(x,y)))\right]
=𝔼pref​(x,y)​[φ⁡(Tθ​(x,y))]+𝔼p+​(x,y)​[φ⁡(Tθ​(x,y))−Tθ​(x,y)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x,y)}\left[\varphi(T_{\theta}(x,y))\right]+\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}(x,y)}\left[\varphi(T_{\theta}(x,y))-T_{\theta}(x,y)\right]
=𝔼p+​(x,y)​[(1+α)​φ​(Tθ​(x,y))−Tθ​(x,y)]+𝔼p−​(x,y)​[(1−α)​φ​(Tθ​(x,y))],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}(x,y)}\left[(1+\alpha)\varphi(T_{\theta}(x,y))-T_{\theta}(x,y)\right]+\mathbb{E}_{p^{-}(x,y)}\left[(1-\alpha)\varphi(T_{\theta}(x,y))\right], (17)

where φ⁡(t)=log⁡(1+exp⁡(t))\varphi(t)=\log(1+\exp(t)) is the softplus function. To obtain the last expression, we used pref​(x,y)=α​p+​(x,y)+(1−α)​p−​(x,y)p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x,y)=\alpha p^{+}(x,y)+(1-\alpha)p^{-}(x,y). Figure 1(b) shows our loss functions for preferred and non-preferred samples. Note that S⁡(t)S(t) used in Eq. (9) can be written as S⁡(t)=−φ⁡(−t)S(t)=-\varphi(-t). This shows that the stabilizing transformation employed in DDRO arises naturally in our approach.

Using the datasets 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+} and 𝒟−\mathcal{D}^{-}, ℒRDRE​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta) is approximated as follows:

ℒRDRO​(θ)≡1N​∑n=1N{(1+α)​φ​(Tθ​(xn+,yn+))−Tθ​(xn+,yn+)}+1M​∑m=1M(1−α)​φ​(Tθ​(xm−,ym−)).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRO}}(\theta)\equiv\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\{(1+\alpha)\varphi(T_{\theta}(x_{n}^{+},y_{n}^{+}))-T_{\theta}(x_{n}^{+},y_{n}^{+})\right\}+\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}(1-\alpha)\varphi(T_{\theta}(x_{m}^{-},y_{m}^{-})). (18)

We optimize this objective by the stochastic optimization method such as AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017). As we will show later, we can omit the KL regularizer used in DDRO, since α\alpha serves as a regularization parameter. We refer to our approach as relative density ratio optimization (RDRO). Algorithm 1 provides the pseudocode for RDRO, and PyTorch implementation is available at Appendix A.

In the following section, we show that our approach is both stable and statistically consistent.

3.2 Stability Analysis

First, we analyze the stability of the proposed method by examining the gradient of the loss function. Since

∇θφ​(Tθ​(x,y))=σ⁡(Tθ​(x,y))​∇θTθ​(x,y)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\varphi(T_{\theta}(x,y))=\sigma(T_{\theta}(x,y))\nabla_{\theta}T_{\theta}(x,y) (19)

and

∇θTθ​(x,y)=∇θ​log​pθ​(y|x),\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}T_{\theta}(x,y)=\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(y|x), (20)

the gradient of ℒRDRE​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta) can be written as follows:

∇θℒRDRE​(θ)=𝔼p+​(x,y)​[cθ+​(x,y)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(y|x)]+𝔼p−​(x,y)​[cθ−​(x,y)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(y|x)],\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}(x,y)}\left[c_{\theta}^{+}(x,y)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(y|x)\right]+\mathbb{E}_{p^{-}(x,y)}\left[c_{\theta}^{-}(x,y)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(y|x)\right], (21)

where

cθ+​(x,y)=(1+α)​σ​(Tθ​(x,y))−1,cθ−​(x,y)=(1−α)​σ​(Tθ​(x,y)).\displaystyle c_{\theta}^{+}(x,y)=(1+\alpha)\sigma(T_{\theta}(x,y))-1,\qquad c_{\theta}^{-}(x,y)=(1-\alpha)\sigma(T_{\theta}(x,y)). (22)

For the preferred dataset 𝒟+\mathcal{D}^{+}, we would like pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) to be large, whereas for the non-preferred dataset 𝒟−\mathcal{D}^{-}, we would like pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) to be small. Thus, cθ+​(x,y)≤0c_{\theta}^{+}(x,y)\leq 0 and cθ−​(x,y)≥0c_{\theta}^{-}(x,y)\geq 0 are required. By definition, cθ−​(x,y)c_{\theta}^{-}(x,y) is always non-negative, and when pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) becomes sufficiently small for the non-preferred data, cθ−​(x,y)c_{\theta}^{-}(x,y) becomes zero.

On the other hand, for cθ+​(x,y)c_{\theta}^{+}(x,y), the following inequality holds:

cθ+​(x,y)≤0⇔rθ​(y|x)≡pθ​(y|x)pref​(y|x)≤1α.\displaystyle c_{\theta}^{+}(x,y)\leq 0\Leftrightarrow r_{\theta}(y|x)\equiv\frac{p_{\theta}(y|x)}{p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)}\leq\frac{1}{\alpha}. (23)

For the preferred data (x+,y+)(x^{+},y^{+}), the gradient is negative when rθ​(y+|x+)≤1/αr_{\theta}(y^{+}|x^{+})\leq 1/\alpha. This enlarges pθ​(y+|x+)p_{\theta}(y^{+}|x^{+}) until cθ+​(x+,y+)c_{\theta}^{+}(x^{+},y^{+}) becomes zero at rθ​(y+|x+)=1/αr_{\theta}(y^{+}|x^{+})=1/\alpha. Hence, the constraint on the relative density ratio, rθ​(y+|x+)∈[0,1/α]r_{\theta}(y^{+}|x^{+})\in[0,1/\alpha], is automatically satisfied.

From another perspective, pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) is trained so that it does not exceed pref​(y|x)/αp_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)/\alpha. When α\alpha is large, pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) remains close to pref​(y|x)p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x), whereas when α\alpha is small, pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x) can deviate from pref​(y|x)p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x). Hence, α\alpha can be interpreted as a regularization parameter.

3.3 Statistical Consistency Analysis

Next, we analyze the statistical consistency of the proposed method. For the optimal parameter θ∗\theta^{*} that minimizes the true risk ℒRDRE(θ)=𝔼pref[Bregf(r∗∥rθ)]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(r^{*}\|r_{\theta}\right)\right], since ff is strictly convex, the following consistency holds:

ℒRDRE​(θ∗)=0⇔rθ∗=r∗⇔pθ∗=p+.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta^{*})=0\Leftrightarrow r_{\theta^{*}}=r^{*}\Leftrightarrow p_{\theta^{*}}=p^{+}. (24)

Although this is an ideal property, since the number of samples is finite in practice, it is necessary to evaluate the convergence rate.

As a preliminary step, we evaluate the Lipschitz constant of the Bregman divergence, which can be rewritten as follows:

Bregf(u∥v)=−f⁡(v)+f′​(v)​v⏟ψ1​(v)+(−f′​(v))⏟ψ2​(v)u+f⁡(u)⏟C​o​n​s​t..\displaystyle\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(u\|v\right)=\underbrace{-f(v)+f^{\prime}(v)v}_{\psi_{1}(v)}+\underbrace{(-f^{\prime}(v))}_{\psi_{2}(v)}u+\underbrace{f(u)}_{Const.}. (25)

Let L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} be the Lipschitz constants of ψ1\psi_{1} and ψ2\psi_{2}, respectively. Then, the Lipschitz constant of the Bregman divergence can be written as follows:

Lip(Bregf(u∥⋅))=L1+(sup|u|)L2.\displaystyle\mathrm{Lip}\left(\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(u\|\cdot\right)\right)=L_{1}+(\sup\left|u\right|)L_{2}. (26)

For the proposed method, since r∗≤1/αr^{*}\leq 1/\alpha, this Lipschitz constant becomes:

CLip=Lip(Bregf(r∗∥⋅))=L1+(sup|r∗|)L2=L1+1αL2.\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{Lip}}=\mathrm{Lip}\left(\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(r^{*}\|\cdot\right)\right)=L_{1}+(\sup\left|r^{*}\right|)L_{2}=L_{1}+\frac{1}{\alpha}L_{2}. (27)

Let Θ\Theta be the parameter set, and ℋ={pθ∣θ∈Θ}\mathcal{H}=\left\{p_{\theta}\mid\theta\in\Theta\right\} be the corresponding model class, following the convention of (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025). For this ℋ\mathcal{H}, the Rademacher complexity (Mohri et al., 2018) is defined as ℛK​(ℋ)\mathcal{R}_{K}(\mathcal{H}), where KK is the number of samples. The Rademacher complexity measures richness of a model class and is commonly used to bound generalization error. Based on this, we evaluate the estimation error of the policy with the true preference.

Theorem 3.1.

Let us define θ^=arg​minθ⁡ℒ^RDRE​(θ)\hat{\theta}=\argmin_{\theta}\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta), where ℒ^RDRE​(θ)\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta) is the empirical approximation of ℒRDRE​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta) by using the datasets 𝒟±={𝒟+,𝒟−}\mathcal{D}^{\pm}=\left\{\mathcal{D}^{+},\mathcal{D}^{-}\right\}. The estimation error of pθ^p_{\hat{\theta}} with p+p^{+} is bounded above as follows:

𝔼𝒟±​[𝔼p+​[(pθ^−p+)2]]≤2α​μ​[infθ∈ΘℒRDRE​(θ)+4​CLip​{α​ℛN​(ℋ)+(1−α)​ℛM​(ℋ)}],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{\pm}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}}\left[\left(p_{\hat{\theta}}-p^{+}\right)^{2}\right]\right]\leq\frac{2}{\alpha\mu}\left[\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)+4C_{\mathrm{Lip}}\left\{\alpha\mathcal{R}_{N}(\mathcal{H})+(1-\alpha)\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathcal{H})\right\}\right], (28)

where μ\mu satisfies f′′​(t)≥μf^{\prime\prime}(t)\geq\mu for all tt.

Proof sketch.

Since ff in Bregman divergence is a strongly convex function, the true risk ℒRDRE​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta) is bounded below as follows:

ℒRDRE(θ)=𝔼pref[Bregf(r∗∥rθ)]≥μ2𝔼pref[(r∗−rθ)2].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(r^{*}\|r_{\theta}\right)\right]\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\left(r^{*}-r_{\theta}\right)^{2}\right]. (29)

Combining this with pθ−p+=pref​(rθ−r∗)p_{\theta}-p^{+}=p_{\mathrm{ref}}(r_{\theta}-r^{*}), p+=r∗​prefp^{+}=r^{*}p_{\mathrm{ref}}, r∗≤1/αr^{*}\leq 1/\alpha, and pref≤1p_{\mathrm{ref}}\leq 1 since prefp_{\mathrm{ref}} is a discrete probability distribution, we obtain:

𝔼p+​[(pθ−p+)2]≤2α​μ​ℒRDRE​(θ).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}}\left[\left(p_{\theta}-p^{+}\right)^{2}\right]\leq\frac{2}{\alpha\mu}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta). (30)

Moreover, for the optimal parameter of the empirical risk ℒ^RDRE​(θ)\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta), the following inequality holds:

ℒRDRE​(θ^)≤infθ∈ΘℒRDRE​(θ)+supθ∈Θ(ℒ^RDRE​(θ)−ℒRDRE​(θ))+supθ∈Θ(ℒRDRE​(θ)−ℒ^RDRE​(θ)).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\hat{\theta})\leq\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)+\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)\right)+\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)-\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)\right). (31)

Using the Rademacher complexity, the second term on the right-hand side can be bounded above as follows:

𝔼𝒟±​[supθ∈Θ(ℒ^RDRE​(θ)−ℒRDRE​(θ))]≤2​CLip​{α​ℛN​(ℋ)+(1−α)​ℛM​(ℋ)}.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{\pm}}\left[\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)\right)\right]\leq 2C_{\mathrm{Lip}}\left\{\alpha\mathcal{R}_{N}(\mathcal{H})+(1-\alpha)\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathcal{H})\right\}. (32)

The third term on the right-hand side can be bounded in the same way. Combining Eqs. (30), (31), and (32), we obtain Theorem 3.1. The detailed proof is given in Appendix B. ∎

Since ℛK​(ℋ)=𝒪⁡(1/K)\mathcal{R}_{K}(\mathcal{H})=\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K}) usually holds (Mohri et al., 2018), the right-hand side of Eq. (28) can be evaluated as

𝒪⁡(infθ∈ΘℒRDRE​(θ)+1/N+1/M).\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\left(\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta)+1/\sqrt{N}+1/\sqrt{M}\right). (33)

In addition, if the model class ℋ\mathcal{H} contains the true preference p+p^{+}, infθ∈ΘℒRDRE​(θ)\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta), the misspecification error between pθp_{\theta} and p+p^{+}, becomes zero. Therefore, 𝔼p+​[(pθ^−p+)2]→0\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}}\left[\left(p_{\hat{\theta}}-p^{+}\right)^{2}\right]\to 0 as N,M→∞N,M\to\infty.

3.4 Comparison of Convergence Rates

Finally, we compare the convergence rates of the proposed method and DDRO. According to (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025), the upper bound of the estimation error for DDRO is:

𝔼𝒟±​[𝔼p+​[(pθ^−p+)2]]≤2​(1−α)2α2​m+2​μ​[infθ∈ΘℒDRE​(θ)+4​CLip′​{ℛN​(ℋ)+ℛM​(ℋ)}],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{\pm}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}}\left[\left(p_{\hat{\theta}}-p^{+}\right)^{2}\right]\right]\leq\frac{2\left(1-\alpha\right)^{2}}{\alpha^{2}m_{+}^{2}\mu}\left[\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DRE}}(\theta)+4C_{\mathrm{Lip}}^{\prime}\left\{\mathcal{R}_{N}(\mathcal{H})+\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathcal{H})\right\}\right], (34)

where

m+=minx∈𝒳,y∈supp(p+(⋅|x))p+(y|x)>0\displaystyle m_{+}=\min_{x\in\mathcal{X},y\in\mathrm{supp}(p^{+}(\cdot|x))}p^{+}(y|x)>0 (35)

is the minimum value of p+​(y|x)p^{+}(y|x) within its support supp(p+(⋅|x))\mathrm{supp}(p^{+}(\cdot|x)), 𝒳\mathcal{X} is the input space, and

CLip′=Lip(Bregf(g∗∥⋅))=L1+(sup|g∗|)L2.\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{Lip}}^{\prime}=\mathrm{Lip}\left(\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(g^{*}\|\cdot\right)\right)=L_{1}+(\sup\left|g^{*}\right|)L_{2}. (36)

We now compare the upper bound of our approach (Eq. (28)) with that of DDRO. Since infθ∈ΘℒDRE​(θ)\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DRE}}(\theta) and infθ∈ΘℒRDRE​(θ)\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta) become zero when the model class ℋ\mathcal{H} contains the true preference p+p^{+}, we compare the remaining terms in the upper bounds.

Since m+≪1m_{+}\ll 1, we expect that the following inequality holds:

2α​μ≪2​(1−α)2α2​m+2​μ.\displaystyle\frac{2}{\alpha\mu}\ll\frac{2\left(1-\alpha\right)^{2}}{\alpha^{2}m_{+}^{2}\mu}. (37)

To justify this, we derive the condition on α\alpha under which the inequality holds. Assuming α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and μ>0\mu>0, we have:

2α​μ<2​(1−α)2α2​m+2​μ⇔α​m+2<(1−α)2⇔α2−(2+m+2)​α+1>0,\displaystyle\frac{2}{\alpha\mu}<\frac{2\left(1-\alpha\right)^{2}}{\alpha^{2}m_{+}^{2}\mu}\Leftrightarrow\alpha m_{+}^{2}<\left(1-\alpha\right)^{2}\Leftrightarrow\alpha^{2}-(2+m_{+}^{2})\alpha+1>0, (38)

which yields:

α<(m+2+4−m+2)2.\displaystyle\alpha<\left(\frac{\sqrt{m_{+}^{2}+4}-m_{+}}{2}\right)^{2}. (39)

Using a Taylor expansion around m+→0m_{+}\rightarrow 0, we obtain

(m+2+4−m+2)2=1−m++O⁡(m+2),\displaystyle\left(\frac{\sqrt{m_{+}^{2}+4}-m_{+}}{2}\right)^{2}=1-m_{+}+O(m_{+}^{2}), (40)

and hence,

α<1−m++O⁡(m+2).\displaystyle\alpha<1-m_{+}+O(m_{+}^{2}). (41)

For any fixed α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), if there exists a sufficiently small m+m_{+}, then Eq. (41) holds. Since m+≪1m_{+}\ll 1, we expect this condition to be satisfied, and therefore, the right-hand side in Eq. (37) can be much larger than the left-hand side.

Moreover, since 1/α≪sup|g∗|1/\alpha\ll\sup\left|g^{*}\right|, the following inequality holds:

CLip=L1+1α​L2≪L1+(sup|g∗|)​L2=CLip′.\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{Lip}}=L_{1}+\frac{1}{\alpha}L_{2}\ll L_{1}+(\sup\left|g^{*}\right|)L_{2}=C_{\mathrm{Lip}}^{\prime}. (42)

In addition, since α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), the following inequality holds:

α​ℛN​(ℋ)+(1−α)​ℛM​(ℋ)≤ℛN​(ℋ)+ℛM​(ℋ).\displaystyle\alpha\mathcal{R}_{N}(\mathcal{H})+(1-\alpha)\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathcal{H})\leq\mathcal{R}_{N}(\mathcal{H})+\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathcal{H}). (43)

From the above discussion, although both the proposed method and DDRO share the order of 𝒪⁡(1/N+1/M)\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N}+1/\sqrt{M}), our coefficient terms are significantly smaller than those for DDRO. In particular, in DDRO, the occurrence of 1/m+1/m_{+} and the potentially large value of sup|g∗|\sup\left|g^{*}\right| arise from the instability of the density ratio g∗∈[0,∞)g^{*}\in\left[0,\infty\right). The proposed method avoids this order deterioration by using the relative density ratio r∗∈[0,1/α]r^{*}\in\left[0,1/\alpha\right] instead of the density ratio g∗g^{*}.

To summarize our contributions, our approach is more stable and statistically consistent, and yields significantly tighter convergence guarantees than DDRO.

4 Related Work

4.1 Alignment

Many alignment methods assume specific human preference models, such as the Bradley-Terry model (Bradley and Terry, 1952) and prospect theory (Tversky and Kahneman, 1992; Kahneman and Tversky, 2013). Among them, the Bradley-Terry model is the most widely used for training reward models (Ouyang et al., 2022; Uesato et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023; Ahmadian et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024). RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022) and its variants (Uesato et al., 2022; Ahmadian et al., 2024) optimize the language model via reinforcement learning to maximize the reward model. In contrast, DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) and its variants (Xu et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024) show that the reward model can be represented by the language model and directly optimize the language model through reward model training. KTO (Ethayarajh et al., 2024) is an alignment method based on prospect theory and can be regarded as a generalization of DPO. Furthermore, while RLHF and DPO require triplet data (x,yw,yl)(x,y_{w},y_{l}) where xx is a prompt, ywy_{w} is a preferred response, and yly_{l} is a non-preferred response, KTO can be applied whenever responses are annotated with binary labels indicating whether they are preferred or not.

Unfortunately, specific human preference models such as the Bradley-Terry model fail to accurately capture true human preferences (Wu et al., 2022). A common failure case is cyclic preference, as described in Appendix C. For instance, there may exist three responses y1,y2,y3y_{1},y_{2},y_{3} to a prompt such that y1y_{1} is preferred over y2y_{2}, y2y_{2} is preferred over y3y_{3}, yet y3y_{3} is preferred over y1y_{1}. The Bradley-Terry model cannot capture these inconsistent human preferences (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025). Since such situations frequently arise in practice, alignment methods that rely on a specific model of human preferences have inherent limitations.

To address these limitations, several approaches have been presented, including those based on energy-based models (Hong et al., 2024), Nash equilibrium (Munos et al., 2023), binary classification (Jung et al., 2024), and density ratio estimation (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025; Kim et al., 2025). In particular, DDRO (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025) has statistical consistency as shown in Section 2.2. However, DDRO is also known to suffer from training instability. This is due to the instability of density ratio estimation. In contrast, our approach offers both training stability and statistical consistency, and yields significantly tighter convergence guarantees than DDRO.

4.2 Relative Density Ratio Estimation

Density ratio estimation (Sugiyama et al., 2012), estimating the ratio of two distributions directly, has a wide range of applications such as covariate shift adaptation (Sugiyama et al., 2007), outlier detection (Hido et al., 2011), change-point detection (Liu et al., 2013), positive-unlabeled learning (Kato et al., 2019; Kato and Teshima, 2021), and generative adversarial networks (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Nowozin et al., 2016).

While various density ratio estimators have been presented, including logistic regression (Hastie et al., 2005), kernel mean matching (Gretton et al., 2009), KL-divergence-based approaches (Sugiyama et al., 2008), and least-squares-based approaches (Kanamori et al., 2009), they can be unified as minimization problems of Bregman divergence (Sugiyama et al., 2012). DDRO (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025) provides a theoretical analysis from the perspective of Bregman divergence, while adopting a logistic regression approach in practice. However, the density ratio may diverge when the supports of the two distributions are different, leading to instability in DDRO.

To address this instability, we employ the relative density ratio (Yamada et al., 2013), which is the generalization of the density ratio. As discussed in Section 3, the relative density ratio is bounded above and does not diverge, enabling more stable estimation. This property enables us to achieve training stability. Analogous to DDRO, we provide a theoretical analysis from the perspective of Bregman divergence, and show that our approach yields significantly tighter convergence guarantees than DDRO. Whereas existing relative density ratio estimators are based on least-squares (Yamada et al., 2013; Kumagai et al., 2021), we adopt logistic regression in practice, since it has been empirically shown to yield better performance.

5 Experiments

To evaluate our approach, we compared it against two state-of-the-art alignment methods: KTO (Ethayarajh et al., 2024) and DDRO (Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025).

5.1 Base Models, Preference Datasets, and Metrics

We applied these alignment methods to the following base models: Qwen 2.5 Instruct (1.5B and 3B) (Team et al., 2024), and Llama 3 Instruct (3B and 8B) (Grattafiori et al., 2024). We refer to them as Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-3B, Llama-3B, and Llama-8B, respectively.

As the preference datasets, we used UltraFeedback GPT-3.5-Turbo Helpfulness (UF-G) and KTO Mix 14K (MIX-14K). UF-G is derived from the UltraFeedback (Cui et al., 2023) and filtered for helpfulness, containing preferred and non-preferred responses to various prompts labeled by GPT-3.5-turbo. MIX-14K mixes the following three datasets: Capybara, Orca, and UltraFeedback by sampling from each source in equal proportions. UF-G contains 6,088 preferred and 9,644 non-preferred samples, while MIX-14K contains 6,750 preferred and 6,750 non-preferred samples.

As the metric, we used AlpacaEval length-controlled (LC) win rates (Dubois et al., 2024). We generated responses from the aligned models on the alpaca_eval prompts, computed win rates against a baseline using an LLM-based auto-annotator, and reported LC win rates that regress out AlpacaEval’s bias toward longer outputs. We used gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09 for the baseline and weighted_alpaca_eval_gpt4_turbo for the auto-annotator.

5.2 Setup

We implemented all methods using the Hugging Face TRL library. We used the KTO implementation in TRL and implemented DDRO and the proposed method by extending this KTO implementation. For training, we used AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017) with a cosine learning rate scheduler (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2016). Following the TRL documentation, we trained all models for one epoch with a learning rate of 5×10−75\times 10^{-7} and a batch size of 128. We set the maximum gradient norm for gradient clipping to 1.0 and used a warmup ratio of 10% of the total training steps.

For DDRO and the proposed method, we set the hyperparameter α\alpha to the fraction of preferred samples in each dataset: 0.39 for UF-G and 0.5 for MIX-14K.

The experiments were conducted on machines equipped with NVIDIA H100 GPUs (80GB HBM3), Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ CPUs, and 2.0TB of memory. We performed distributed training over 8 GPUs using Hugging Face Accelerate and enabled memory-efficient training with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 (Rajbhandari et al., 2020). We repeated each experiment three times with different random seeds.

5.3 Results

Tables 1 and 2 show the AlpacaEval LC win rates on UF-G and MIX-14K, respectively. We used boldface to indicate the best results and statistically non-different results according to a pairwise t-test with a significance level of 5%.

We first focus on the results on UF-G. Table 1 shows that, across all models, the proposed method achieves performance comparable to or better than both KTO and DDRO. In particular, for Llama-3B and Llama-8B, the proposed method yields a statistically significant improvement over KTO and DDRO.

We next focus on the results on MIX-14K. Table 2 shows that, across all models, the proposed method achieves comparable performance to KTO and DDRO.

These differences in results may be due to differences in the properties of the datasets. MIX-14K is derived from DPO-Mix-7K, which was originally created for DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023), and consists of triplet samples (x,yw,yl)(x,y_{w},y_{l}), where xx is a prompt, ywy_{w} is a preferred response, and yly_{l} is a non-preferred response. MIX-14K decomposes each triplet sample into two prompt and response pairs: (x,yw)(x,y_{w}) and (x,yl)(x,y_{l}). That is, for every prompt, both a preferred and a non-preferred response are always available. This makes alignment on MIX-14K relatively easy, and hence, all alignment methods achieve competitive performance.

On the other hand, UF-G does not have this property: for a given prompt xx, only one of ywy_{w} or yly_{l} is available. This makes alignment on UF-G more challenging and may result in larger performance differences among alignment methods. In practice, it is difficult to always provide both preferred and non-preferred responses for each prompt. Therefore, achieving strong performance on realistic datasets like UF-G is particularly important. Additional results on BIG-Bench Hard (Suzgun et al., 2023) are provided in Appendix D.

5.4 Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis

Finally, we investigated the sensitivity of the hyperparameter α\alpha in the proposed method. Figures 2(a), 2(b), 2(c), and 2(d) show the relationship between AlpacaEval LC win rates and α\alpha for Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-3B, Llama-3B, and Llama-8B on UF-G, respectively. Overall, performance varies only slightly with α\alpha, indicating stable behavior of the proposed method. Based on these results, we recommend setting α\alpha to the fraction of preferred samples in each dataset. The results on MIX-14K are provided in Figures 3(a), 3(b), 3(c), and 3(d). On MIX-14K, there was no statistically significant difference between RDRO and DDRO for most values of α\alpha.

These results indicate that the proposed method performs robustly across a range of base models and datasets, and is a promising alternative to KTO and DDRO. We also provide an empirical analysis of the training dynamics of the proposed method in Appendix E.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose a novel alignment method called relative density ratio optimization (RDRO), which is more stable and statistically consistent, and yields significantly tighter convergence guarantees than DDRO. Experiments across various models and datasets demonstrate that our RDRO achieves performance comparable to or better than KTO and DDRO.

Appendix A PyTorch Implementation

RDRO is easy to implement in practice; PyTorch code for the RDRO loss is provided below:

import torch
from torch.nn.functional import softplus


def rdro_loss(
    policy_chosen_logps,
    policy_rejected_logps,
    reference_chosen_logps,
    reference_rejected_logps,
    alpha,
):
    """
    policy_chosen_logps: policy logprobs for chosen responses
    policy_rejected_logps: policy logprobs for rejected responses
    reference_chosen_logps: reference policy logprobs for chosen responses
    reference_rejected_logps: reference policy logprobs for rejected responses
    alpha: hyperparameter in (0, 1)
    """

    chosen_logratios = policy_chosen_logps - reference_chosen_logps
    chosen_losses = (1 + alpha) * softplus(chosen_logratios) - chosen_logratios

    rejected_logratios = policy_rejected_logps - reference_rejected_logps
    rejected_losses = (1 - alpha) * softplus(rejected_logratios)

    return torch.cat([chosen_losses, rejected_losses], dim=0)

Appendix B Proof of Theorem 3.1

In this section, we will prove Theorem 3.1 after providing four relevant lemmas. For simplicity, we denote the true risk ℒRDRE​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta) as ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta), and the empirical risk ℒ^RDRE​(θ)\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{RDRE}}(\theta) as ℒ^​(θ)\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta).

Lemma B.1.

ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta) is bounded below as follows:

ℒ(θ)=𝔼pref[Bregf(r∗∥rθ)]≥μ2𝔼pref[(r∗−rθ)2],\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(r^{*}\|r_{\theta}\right)\right]\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\left(r^{*}-r_{\theta}\right)^{2}\right], (44)

where μ\mu satisfies f′′​(t)≥μf^{\prime\prime}(t)\geq\mu for all tt.

Proof.

Since ff is a strongly convex function, the following inequality holds:

f⁡(r∗)≥f⁡(rθ)+f′​(rθ)​(r∗−rθ)+μ2​(r∗−rθ)2,\displaystyle f(r^{*})\geq f(r_{\theta})+f^{\prime}(r_{\theta})(r^{*}-r_{\theta})+\frac{\mu}{2}\left(r^{*}-r_{\theta}\right)^{2}, (45)

and thus,

Bregf(r∗∥rθ)=f(r∗)−f(rθ)−f′(rθ)(r∗−rθ)≥μ2(r∗−rθ)2.\displaystyle\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(r^{*}\|r_{\theta}\right)=f(r^{*})-f(r_{\theta})-f^{\prime}(r_{\theta})(r^{*}-r_{\theta})\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\left(r^{*}-r_{\theta}\right)^{2}. (46)

Taking expectations on both sides yields the claim. ∎

Lemma B.2.

The squared error between pθp_{\theta} and p+p^{+} can be bounded by ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta) as follows:

𝔼p+​[(pθ−p+)2]≤2α​μ​ℒ​(θ).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}}\left[\left(p_{\theta}-p^{+}\right)^{2}\right]\leq\frac{2}{\alpha\mu}\mathcal{L}(\theta). (47)
Proof.

The squared error between pθp_{\theta} and p+p^{+} is bounded above as follows:

𝔼p+​[(pθ−p+)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}}\left[\left(p_{\theta}-p^{+}\right)^{2}\right] =𝔼p+​[pref2​(rθ−r∗)2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}}\left[p_{\mathrm{ref}}^{2}\left(r_{\theta}-r^{*}\right)^{2}\right] (48)
=𝔼pref​[r∗​pref2​(rθ−r∗)2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[r^{*}p_{\mathrm{ref}}^{2}\left(r_{\theta}-r^{*}\right)^{2}\right] (49)
≤1α​𝔼pref​[pref2​(rθ−r∗)2]\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[p_{\mathrm{ref}}^{2}\left(r_{\theta}-r^{*}\right)^{2}\right] (50)
≤1α​𝔼pref​[(rθ−r∗)2],\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\left(r_{\theta}-r^{*}\right)^{2}\right], (51)

where we used pθ−p+=pref​(rθ−r∗)p_{\theta}-p^{+}=p_{\mathrm{ref}}(r_{\theta}-r^{*}), p+=r∗​prefp^{+}=r^{*}p_{\mathrm{ref}}, r∗≤1/αr^{*}\leq 1/\alpha, and pref≤1p_{\mathrm{ref}}\leq 1 since prefp_{\mathrm{ref}} is a discrete probability distribution. Combining with Lemma B.1 yields the claim. ∎

Lemma B.3.

For θ^\hat{\theta} that satisfies θ^=arg​minθ⁡ℒ^​(θ)\hat{\theta}=\argmin_{\theta}\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta), ℒ⁡(θ^)\mathcal{L}(\hat{\theta}) is bounded above as follows:

ℒ⁡(θ^)≤infθ∈Θℒ⁡(θ)+supθ∈Θ(ℒ⁡(θ)−ℒ^​(θ))+supθ∈Θ(ℒ^​(θ)−ℒ⁡(θ)).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\hat{\theta})\leq\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)+\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\mathcal{L}(\theta)-\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)\right)+\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)-\mathcal{L}(\theta)\right). (52)
Proof.

ℒ⁡(θ^)\mathcal{L}(\hat{\theta}) is bounded above as follows:

ℒ⁡(θ^)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\hat{\theta}) =ℒ⁡(θ^)+ℒ⁡(θ)−ℒ⁡(θ)+ℒ^​(θ^)−ℒ^​(θ^)+ℒ^​(θ)−ℒ^​(θ)\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}(\hat{\theta})+\mathcal{L}(\theta)-\mathcal{L}(\theta)+\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\hat{\theta})-\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\hat{\theta})+\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)-\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta) (53)
=ℒ⁡(θ)+(ℒ⁡(θ^)−ℒ^​(θ^))+(ℒ^​(θ)−ℒ⁡(θ))+(ℒ^​(θ^)−ℒ^​(θ))\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}(\theta)+\left(\mathcal{L}(\hat{\theta})-\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\hat{\theta})\right)+\left(\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)-\mathcal{L}(\theta)\right)+\left(\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\hat{\theta})-\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)\right) (54)
≤ℒ⁡(θ)+supθ∈Θ(ℒ⁡(θ)−ℒ^​(θ))+supθ∈Θ(ℒ^​(θ)−ℒ⁡(θ)),\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{L}(\theta)+\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\mathcal{L}(\theta)-\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)\right)+\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)-\mathcal{L}(\theta)\right), (55)

where we used ℒ^​(θ^)−ℒ^​(θ)≤0\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\hat{\theta})-\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)\leq 0. Taking the infimum over θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta on both sides yields the claim. ∎

Lemma B.4.

The uniform deviation between the empirical risk ℒ^​(θ)\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta) and the true risk ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta) is bounded above as follows:

𝔼𝒟±​[supθ∈Θ(ℒ^​(θ)−ℒ⁡(θ))]≤2​CLip​{α​ℛN​(ℋ)+(1−α)​ℛM​(ℋ)},\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{\pm}}\left[\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)-\mathcal{L}(\theta)\right)\right]\leq 2C_{\mathrm{Lip}}\left\{\alpha\mathcal{R}_{N}(\mathcal{H})+(1-\alpha)\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathcal{H})\right\}, (56)

where 𝒟±={𝒟+,𝒟−}\mathcal{D}^{\pm}=\left\{\mathcal{D}^{+},\mathcal{D}^{-}\right\} is the dataset, CLipC_{\mathrm{Lip}} is the Lipschitz constant of the Bregman divergence, and ℛN​(ℋ)\mathcal{R}_{N}(\mathcal{H}) and ℛM​(ℋ)\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathcal{H}) are Rademacher complexities of the model class ℋ={pθ∣θ∈Θ}\mathcal{H}=\left\{p_{\theta}\mid\theta\in\Theta\right\} with sample sizes NN and MM, respectively.

Proof.

Let z=(x,y)z=(x,y) and define ℓθ(z)≡Bregf(r∗(z)∥rθ(z))\ell_{\theta}(z)\equiv\mathrm{Breg}_{f}\left(r^{*}(z)\|r_{\theta}(z)\right). With this notation, we can rewrite ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta) and ℒ^​(θ)\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta) as follows:

ℒ⁡(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta) =α​𝔼p+​[ℓθ​(z)]+(1−α)​𝔼p−​[ℓθ​(z)],\displaystyle=\alpha\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}}\left[\ell_{\theta}(z)\right]+(1-\alpha)\mathbb{E}_{p^{-}}\left[\ell_{\theta}(z)\right], (57)
ℒ^​(θ)\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta) =α​1N​∑n=1Nℓθ​(zn+)+(1−α)​1M​∑m=1Mℓθ​(zm−),\displaystyle=\alpha\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell_{\theta}(z_{n}^{+})+(1-\alpha)\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\ell_{\theta}(z_{m}^{-}), (58)

where (zn+)n=1N=(xn+,yn+)n=1N=𝒟+\left(z_{n}^{+}\right)_{n=1}^{N}=\left(x_{n}^{+},y_{n}^{+}\right)_{n=1}^{N}=\mathcal{D}^{+} and (zm−)m=1M=(xm−,ym−)m=1M=𝒟−\left(z_{m}^{-}\right)_{m=1}^{M}=\left(x_{m}^{-},y_{m}^{-}\right)_{m=1}^{M}=\mathcal{D}^{-}. Then, we obtain the following inequality:

supθ∈Θ(ℒ^​(θ)−ℒ⁡(θ))≤α​supθ∈Θ(1N​∑n=1Nℓθ​(zn+)−𝔼p+​[ℓθ​(z)])+(1−α)​supθ∈Θ(1M​∑m=1Mℓθ​(zm−)−𝔼p−​[ℓθ​(z)]).\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)-\mathcal{L}(\theta)\right)\leq\alpha\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell_{\theta}(z_{n}^{+})-\mathbb{E}_{p^{+}}\left[\ell_{\theta}(z)\right]\right)+(1-\alpha)\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\ell_{\theta}(z_{m}^{-})-\mathbb{E}_{p^{-}}\left[\ell_{\theta}(z)\right]\right). (59)

By the symmetrization trick [Mohri et al., 2018] and the contraction inequality [Mohri et al., 2018], the uniform deviation is bounded above as follows:

𝔼𝒟±​[supθ∈Θ(ℒ^​(θ)−ℒ⁡(θ))]≤2​CLip​{α​ℛN​(ℋ)+(1−α)​ℛM​(ℋ)},\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}^{\pm}}\left[\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left(\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)-\mathcal{L}(\theta)\right)\right]\leq 2C_{\mathrm{Lip}}\left\{\alpha\mathcal{R}_{N}(\mathcal{H})+(1-\alpha)\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathcal{H})\right\}, (60)

ℛK​(ℋ)=𝔼𝒟​[𝔼σ​[supθ∈Θ1K​∑k=1Kσk​pθ​(zk)]]\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{K}(\mathcal{H})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sigma_{k}p_{\theta}(z_{k})\right]\right] (61)

≤2α​μ​[infθ∈Θℒ⁡(θ)+4​CLip​{α​ℛN​(ℋ)+(1−α)​ℛM​(ℋ)}].\displaystyle\leq\frac{2}{\alpha\mu}\left[\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)+4C_{\mathrm{Lip}}\left\{\alpha\mathcal{R}_{N}(\mathcal{H})+(1-\alpha)\mathcal{R}_{M}(\mathcal{H})\right\}\right]. (66)

Appendix C Canonical Violation of Bradley-Terry Assumption

Under the Bradley-Terry assumption, for two responses y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} to a prompt xx, the probability that y1y_{1} is preferred over y2y_{2} is defined as follows:

Prϕ​(y1≻y2|x)\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}_{\phi}(y_{1}\succ y_{2}|x) =σ⁡(Rϕ​(x,y1)−Rϕ​(x,y2)),\displaystyle=\sigma(R_{\phi}(x,y_{1})-R_{\phi}(x,y_{2})), (67)

where Rϕ​(x,y)R_{\phi}(x,y) denotes the reward model. Now consider a prompt xx with three responses yay_{a}, yby_{b}, ycy_{c} and assume a cyclic preference pattern:

Prϕ​(ya≻yb∣x)=Prϕ​(yb≻yc∣x)=Prϕ​(yc≻ya∣x)=t≠12.\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}_{\phi}(y_{a}\succ y_{b}\mid x)=\mathrm{Pr}_{\phi}(y_{b}\succ y_{c}\mid x)=\mathrm{Pr}_{\phi}(y_{c}\succ y_{a}\mid x)=t\neq\tfrac{1}{2}. (68)

Under the Bradley-Terry assumption, this would require

Rϕ​(x,ya)−Rϕ​(x,yb)=Rϕ​(x,yb)−Rϕ​(x,yc)=Rϕ​(x,yc)−Rϕ​(x,ya).\displaystyle R_{\phi}(x,y_{a})-R_{\phi}(x,y_{b})=R_{\phi}(x,y_{b})-R_{\phi}(x,y_{c})=R_{\phi}(x,y_{c})-R_{\phi}(x,y_{a}). (69)

Taking the sum of these three equalities yields 00, and hence each difference must be zero. Therefore, Pr⁡(ya≻yb∣x)=σ⁡(0)=1/2\mathrm{Pr}(y_{a}\succ y_{b}\mid x)=\sigma(0)=1/2, contradicting the assumption t≠1/2t\neq 1/2.

Appendix D Additional Results on BIG-Bench Hard

As additional experiments, we evaluate the aligned models on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) [Suzgun et al., 2023], which is a benchmark for evaluating the reasoning capabilities of language models. We used the lm-evaluation-harness, where we set the number of fewshot examples to 3.

Tables 3 and 4 show the BBH results on UF-G and MIX-14K, respectively. We used boldface to indicate the best results and statistically non-different results according to a pairwise t-test with a significance level of 5%.

RDRO achieves the best or statistically comparable performance across all models and datasets, with the sole exception of Qwen-3B on MIX-14K. This indicates that RDRO performs equal to or better than DDRO across multiple benchmarks. Note that for Qwen-3B, scores are generally low on BBH across all methods and datasets, including the base model before alignment, suggesting that it is not well-suited to this benchmark.

Appendix E Empirical Analysis of Training Dynamics

In this section, we present the training dynamics over steps (within an epoch), including training losses (Figure 4), gradient norms (Figure 5), and log-ratio trajectories (Figures 6 and 7). Here, log-ratios are defined as the difference between the log-probabilities of the target policy and the reference policy. Figure 6 shows the log-ratios for preferred data, and Figure 7 shows the log-ratios for non-preferred data. We use Llama-8B on UF-G with α=0.39\alpha=0.39.

DDRO introduces heuristic stabilization (e.g., the softplus transformation described in Eq. (9)) to prevent gradient explosion, as also observed in Figure 3 of [Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025]. As a result, gradient norms appear small and training seems stable. However, these modifications change the original objective and may lead to a mismatch with its theoretical properties. Indeed, DDRO exhibits large changes in both preferred and non-preferred log-ratios, indicating overly large deviations from the reference policy. Prior work has shown that overly large deviations from the reference policy can degrade performance [Kwa et al., 2024], and our observations are consistent with this phenomenon. While one might expect that tuning the KL regularization parameter β\beta could mitigate this issue, Appendix D of [Higuchi and Suzuki, 2025] explicitly states that the KL regularization is not included in the gradient calculation for training stability. This suggests that controlling such deviations within DDRO is non-trivial.

In contrast, RDRO does not rely on heuristic stabilization. The softplus transformation employed in DDRO arises naturally in our formulation, while preserving statistical consistency. As shown in Figure 5, although RDRO may exhibit larger gradient norms than heuristic-stabilized DDRO or KTO, it avoids the gradient explosion observed in the original DDRO formulation. Moreover, RDRO avoids overly aggressive updates in both preferred and non-preferred log-ratios, while consistently improving their separation (log-ratio margin), indicating controlled alignment behavior.

Overall, RDRO may appear less stable if stability is interpreted as having small gradient norms. However, we argue that stability should instead be understood as (i) avoiding gradient explosion and (ii) preventing overly large deviations from the reference policy. Under this notion, RDRO provides more principled and stable optimization behavior, consistent with both our theoretical guarantees and empirical observations.

Appendix F Limitations and Future Work

Our approach requires a dataset in which all examples are labeled as either preferred or non-preferred. However, in practice, it is not always possible to obtain such fully labeled data. An important direction for future work is to enable the use of unlabeled data. For instance, one possible approach is to incorporate ideas from positive-unlabeled learning [Kato et al., 2019, Kato and Teshima, 2021].
